title: Do Generate–Verify–Repair Guards Improve LLM NetOps Outputs? A Paired Emulator Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=200 natural-language NetOps intents) to evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline that pairs a hosted LLM with a deterministic network verifier and bounded deterministic repairs improves the rate of emulator-executable network configurations relative to ungated LLM generation. Tasks targeted small single- and multi-device changes (ACLs, MTU/VLAN and admin state sequences) and were executed against a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator and a deterministic validator. Using gpt-5-mini for generation, baseline ungated generation produced 199/200 emulator-executable configurations; the GVR guarded pipeline produced 200/200. The paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005 (95% CI 0.0–0.015); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Predeclared confirmatory hypothesis of a meaningful improvement (≥15 pp) was not supported. Exploratory logs show only a single invocation of the deterministic repair stage. We discuss implications for when GVR guarding is likely to provide operational value, and we report preregistration identifiers, execution manifest summaries, and limitations (synthetic task set, single model, emulator scope).

sections.introduction: Network operators increasingly investigate large language models (LLMs) to translate high-level intents into device configurations, perform limited self-healing, and accelerate NetOps tasks. Fluent but incorrect LLM outputs (hallucinations, structural or semantic errors) pose operational risk because configurations may violate reachability, safety, or workflow constraints. Prior work proposes pairing LLMs with deterministic verifiers, grounding layers, or repair loops to reduce such risks. We preregistered a focused confirmatory study to ask: Does a bounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline materially increase the proportion of emulator-executable configurations produced from natural-language NetOps intents compared with ungated LLM generation? Our contribution is an autonomy-locked, preregistered, paired experiment with machine-verifiable artifacts that quantifies GVR impact on a targeted NetOps task suite and documents practical failure modes and limitations.
sections.related_work: LLM-driven intent-to-configuration translation and NetOps assistants have been studied in recent literature, demonstrating promise on translation and synthesis tasks but also recurring failure modes (hallucination, schema violations) that undermine execution safety [Nguyen et al., 2024; OpsEval, RCACopilot]. Domain-grounding and verifier-augmented architectures (live schema grounding for NL2SQL, retrieval-augmented generation, tool-augmented verification) reduce but do not eliminate hallucinations and have been proposed as practical mitigations [SAL NL2SQL; RAG mitigation surveys]. Formal and automated network verifiers (NetKAT variants, weighted NetKAT, ensemble verifiers) are available to check reachability and safety properties and are natural validators in generation pipelines, though scalability and runtime fidelity remain practical concerns [Weighted NetKAT]. Architecture-level NetOps proposals emphasize that operational reliability depends on verifier contracts, evidence traces, and guarded execution rather than on raw LLM capability alone. Our study builds on this prior work by empirically measuring a bounded GVR pipeline's incremental benefit under a preregistered paired design.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: We preregistered study cnd-001-5f3a before execution (preregistration_sha256: e5c5fdbd717c2c05118643e1d7d5f44055f6356dcf2083bd47c5766cf780ff68). Design: paired confirmatory design with 200 curated natural-language change intents (single- and small multi-device scenarios such as controlled MTU/VLAN migrations, uplink switchover) sampled from a synthetic intent generator. Arms: (A) baseline ungated LLM generation; (B) guarded GVR pipeline: shared initial generation, deterministic validation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and at most one deterministic repair iteration per preregistration. Primary estimand: paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) where success = emulator-executable configuration. Model and tooling: gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses), Dockerized Mininet + FRR emulator, deterministic validator v5. Execution contract limited model calls (maximum 400; used 201) and fixed seeds for deterministic components. Analysis plan: McNemar test for paired binary outcomes (α=0.05) with bootstrap CIs; secondary exploratory taxonomies recorded in artifact logs. All prompts, provider traces, validator traces, and artifacts were archived and hashed as described in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Completed episodes: 400 model-condition episodes (200 paired intents) with no provider failures and full artifact capture. Outcomes: baseline (ungated) produced 199 emulator-executable configurations; guarded GVR produced 200 emulator-executable configurations. Contingency counts: n11=199, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0 (notation: n_guarded,baseline). Paired estimate = 0.005 (guarded − baseline). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired 95% CI (paired-bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.0, 0.015]. Provider-call audit shows a single repair invocation (repair stage count = 1). No episodes required additional retries outside the preregistered retry policy. Secondary analyses predeclared (repair-iteration yields, failure taxonomies) were limited by the near-ceiling success rates; there were effectively no uncorrected failures to analyze in the confirmatory set.
sections.discussion: The preregistered GVR pipeline produced an absolute improvement of 0.5 percentage points (1/200) over ungated LLM outputs in this study; this difference is not statistically significant and does not approach the predeclared target effect (15 pp). Practical interpretation: for the selected synthetic intent family and the tested model (gpt-5-mini), ungated generation already yielded near-perfect emulator-executable configurations under the chosen emulator/verifier fidelity and task constraints. The guarded pipeline applied deterministic repair only once, suggesting that (a) many intents were straightforward for the model or (b) the synthetic tasks favored cases where schema/sequence constraints aligned well with the model's training distribution. This outcome does not imply GVR architectures are unnecessary in general: prior work and domain experience show they reduce hallucinations and structural errors in harder or out-of-distribution settings. Instead, our result highlights that the incremental value of guarding is task-, model-, and environment-dependent. Operational implications: teams should evaluate GVR costs versus expected benefit on production-representative workloads; where LLM baseline correctness is already high, heavy guarding may yield limited marginal returns but still adds assurance and auditability. Reproducibility: all prompts, responses, validator traces, and hashes are archived in the artifact bundle; analysis code and manifests are provided.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, autonomy-locked paired experiment to measure whether a bounded generate–verify–repair pipeline improves the emulator-executable success rate for LLM-generated NetOps configurations. On our curated synthetic task suite and using gpt-5-mini with a deterministic validator, ungated LLM generation already achieved 199/200 success; the guarded pipeline yielded 200/200. The confirmatory hypothesis of a substantial GVR improvement was not supported in this setup. The study underscores that the marginal benefit of GVR depends strongly on task difficulty, model capability, and validator/emulator fidelity. Future work should evaluate GVR gains on broader, production-representative workloads (multivendor CLIs, dynamic control-plane interactions, adversarial intents) and measure additional operational axes (verification latency, rollback efficacy, human-in-the-loop attention cost).

disclosure_statement: This study was executed under autonomy lock specified by the initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human input before the lock was limited to (i) selecting the topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and (ii) approving the master prompt and autonomy boundary; no human manual editing of technical content, figures, captions, references, or results occurred after the lock. The autonomous pipeline performed literature search, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer-review-like internal checks, and manuscript drafting. Models and tools: generation used gpt-5-mini via provider openai_responses (declared in model_configuration.json); deterministic validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5; execution used a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator. Orchestration and adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: study cnd-001-5f3a (preregistration manifest SHA-256: e5c5fdbd717c2c05118643e1d7d5f44055f6356dcf2083bd47c5766cf780ff68) froze the primary estimand, sampling plan (n=200 paired intents), model budget (≤400 calls), repair budget (≤1 repair iteration per intent in the final confirmatory contract), analysis plan (McNemar paired binary test), retry policy (single automatic retry for transient provider errors), and contamination/missingness rules. Execution: completed 400 episodes (200 paired intents) with 201 model calls and no provider/API failures; full artifact bundle, provider traces, validator outputs, and hashes are archived under the execution manifest. Pre-lock development artifacts and rehearsal runs informed infrastructure but were excluded from confirmatory evidence as required by the autonomy boundary. All deviations from preregistration are recorded in the execution manifest; none altered the primary estimand or sample size. No manual post-lock revisions of results or manuscript technical content were performed.
limitations: Synthetic, curated task set focused on small single- and multi-device changes; not a comprehensive coverage of real production NetOps workloads.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) evaluated; results do not imply multi-model generality.

Emulator (Dockerized Mininet+FRR) and deterministic validator provide high-fidelity checks for the selected tasks but do not fully capture production control-plane dynamics, live BGP convergence timing, vendor-specific CLI idiosyncrasies, or hardware-induced behaviors.
Preregistered repair budget limited to a single deterministic repair iteration in the confirmatory protocol; different repair strategies or more iterations might yield different outcomes.
Near-ceiling baseline success limited the power to study GVR failure-mode distributions; exploratory failure-taxonomy conclusions are therefore constrained.
Adversarial or out-of-distribution intents (e.g., prompt-jailbreaks, malformed or ambiguous intents) were not the focus of this confirmatory set and require separate evaluation.
